subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.section_ref: Where I Begin, Where I Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Where I Begin, Where I Flow — Students examine the river map and name the states Godavari flows through, a dam, and a wildlife sanctuary along its course (p. 22)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of the Godavari river on p. 22

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the opening poem aloud slowly; students follow along in Textbook p. 22 and are invited to listen for where the river says it begins and where it ends. A brief whole-class share — what did the river 'tell' us about itself? — surfaces first impressions without correction.

Students study the Godavari river map on Textbook p. 22 in pairs. Together they trace the river's path with a finger, noting its source at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats, the tributaries that join it, and the Bay of Bengal at its mouth. Each pair calls out one feature they spotted; the teacher builds a shared list on the board: states, one dam, one wildlife sanctuary, and one tributary.

Individually, students answer the three map questions in their notebooks: the states the Godavari flows through, a dam and a wildlife sanctuary along its length, and the smaller rivers that join it. The teacher circulates and prompts students who are uncertain to return to the map rather than guess.

Whole-class share-out: the teacher reads each question and cold-calls two or three students. Responses are compared — do different pairs name different tributaries? The teacher closes by connecting the idea of 'second longest river in India' and 'Dakshina Ganga' to the geographical scale students just traced.

periods.implied_lo: Students can extract and record geographical features of a river system from a labelled map.
periods.section_context: Godavari river source at Trimbakeshwar, Western Ghats; tributaries; states the river flows through; dam along Godavari; wildlife sanctuary along Godavari; Bay of Bengal delta; Godavari as Dakshina Ganga; Godavari Pushkaram festival at Nashik.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think this river is called Dakshina Ganga — what does that name tell you about how people think of it?' This naturally draws out the river's sacred and cultural significance alongside its geography.

periods.activity_title: Perennial or Seasonal? Sorting Rivers by Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Where I Begin, Where I Flow — Students examine the river map and name the states Godavari flows through, a dam, and a wildlife sanctuary along its course (p. 22)
materials: Textbook (open to the Godavari section, p. 22)
Two small labels or sticky notes per pair: 'Perennial' and 'Seasonal'
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch: two river outlines, one flowing all year, one dry in summer

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws two quick river outlines on the board — one with water throughout and one with a dry stretch — and asks: 'Which of these would you build your home near, and why?' Students discuss briefly in pairs before sharing with the class. The teacher introduces the terms perennial and seasonal without defining them fully yet.

Students read the relevant portion of the section on perennial versus seasonal rivers and the Godavari's forest ecosystem silently from their textbooks. They then discuss with a partner: what animals and plants does the Godavari forest hold, and what might happen to them if the river stopped flowing? The teacher listens and notes interesting ideas to draw out in the whole-class discussion.

Whole-class discussion: the teacher revisits the board sketches and asks students to tell the class which sketch represents Godavari and why. Students use the vocabulary — perennial, tributary, delta, mangrove — from the section. The teacher presses for precision: 'What is the difference between the delta and the rest of the river's course?'

Students write three sentences in their notebooks: one defining perennial river, one naming two living things the Godavari forest supports, and one explaining why the Coringa Mangrove Forest is special. The teacher circulates and prompts students to use the textbook section to check their own accuracy.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between perennial and seasonal river systems and identify the ecosystems a perennial river sustains.
periods.section_context: Perennial river; seasonal river; Godavari forest; tiger, barking deer, Indian golden gecko, red sandalwood; Godavari delta; Coringa Mangrove Forests; freshwater meeting the sea.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you ever seen a stream or nalla near your home that dries up in summer? What happens to the animals and plants around it when that happens?' This connects the perennial–seasonal distinction to students' own lived landscape.

periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Students explain why people have always built homes near rivers or water bodies (p. 24)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of river-bank settlement and agriculture (p. 24–25)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 24 and look at the illustration of a river-bank settlement in silence for a short while. The teacher then asks: 'What do you notice about where these houses and fields are — what is common to all of them?' Students share observations; the teacher does not confirm or correct yet.

The teacher poses the question from Textbook p. 24: 'Since ancient times, people have always built their homes near rivers or water bodies — can you guess why?' Students first write a personal response in their notebooks, then share with a partner. The teacher circulates and listens for reasoning beyond 'water for drinking', encouraging students to think about farming, transport, and washing.

Whole-class discussion: the teacher builds a board list of reasons students offer. Students are then asked to look at Textbook p. 25 and check: which of our board reasons does the section confirm? Are there any uses the textbook mentions that the class missed? Students add to their notebook responses.

Students write a short response: 'List three ways in which people are dependent on the river Godavari' (Textbook p. 25). The teacher prompts a brief share-out and closes by asking whether rivers near students' own homes or towns are used in similar ways.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why human settlements historically developed near rivers by identifying the essential resources a river provides.
periods.section_context: River as source of drinking water, cooking water, washing water, irrigation water, industrial water; canals and pipes distributing river water; river-bank settlements; Godavari and towns and villages along its course.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone live near a river, canal, or lake? What do the people around it use it for?' This grounds the historical pattern in students' immediate experience before the textbook confirms it.

periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Students identify occupations people are engaged in near the river Godavari and the crops visible near it (p. 25)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of occupations and crops along the Godavari (p. 25–26)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 25–26 and study the illustrations of life along the Godavari in silence. The teacher asks them to notice — without writing yet — every occupation and every crop they can spot in the images. After a quiet observation period, two or three students name what they saw.

Students record their observations in a simple two-column table in their notebooks: one column for 'Occupations near Godavari' and one for 'Crops near Godavari'. They use Textbook p. 25 to identify occupations and Textbook p. 26 to identify crops. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How does each occupation you listed depend on the river directly?'

Pairs compare their tables and discuss the personal-connection question from Textbook p. 26: 'Which crops grow in your region? Where does the water for irrigation come from?' Students write a brief answer reflecting their own regional knowledge. The teacher invites two or three students to share — responses are expected to vary by region and all are affirmed.

The teacher leads a short whole-class summary: which occupations are linked to the river directly (fishing, farming) and which are linked more indirectly (ecotourism)? Students add any missed occupations to their tables. The teacher closes by noting that the same river supports very different kinds of work along its long course.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the range of livelihoods and agricultural practices that depend directly on a river system.
periods.section_context: Agriculture (rice cultivation); fishing; ecotourism; drinking water supply; irrigation via canals; industrial water use; crops near Godavari; occupations near Godavari.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students share regional crops and water sources, ask: 'Is the water for your region's farms from a river, a well, or rain — and does it run all year?' This opens a near-to-far comparison between the Godavari context and students' own agricultural landscapes.

periods.section_ref: The Many Ways I Support Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: The Many Ways I Support Lives — Students make a poster showing all the ways rivers help people, including drawings of homes, farms, boats, and fishermen (p. 26)
materials: Large paper or the back of an old calendar sheet per group

time_bands.activity: The teacher explains the poster task from Textbook p. 26: each group will make a single poster showing all the ways rivers help people — homes, farms, boats, fishermen, and more. Groups of four are formed quickly. The teacher sets the expectation: every member of the group must contribute at least one drawing or label to the poster.

Groups plan and create their posters. Each group divides the paper into zones — one zone per major use of rivers — and populates each zone with drawings and short labels. The teacher moves from group to group, pressing with prompts: 'You have fishing and farming — what about the water that reaches your home through pipes? What about electricity from dams?' Students add details as they discuss within the group.

Two or three groups display their posters and one spokesperson from each explains one zone of the poster to the class. Listeners are invited to ask one question or suggest one addition. The teacher notes on the board any river use that appears on most posters versus ones only one group thought of.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'The use of the river that I had not thought of before making this poster is ___.' The teacher collects this as a quick formative check of what the activity surfaced.

periods.implied_lo: Students can communicate multiple ways a river system supports human life through a visual and labelled creative product.
periods.section_context: All ways rivers help people: drinking water, cooking, washing, irrigation, fishing, farming (rice), ecotourism, industrial use, homes near rivers, boats, fishermen.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'Have you included anything your grandparents or people in your village might have used the river for that people do not use it for as much today?' This draws out older cultural and traditional uses of rivers alongside modern ones.

periods.section_ref: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow
periods.textbook_anchor: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow — Students discuss what problems can arise after a dam is built and how they can be solved (p. 27)
periods.visual_aids: Board T-chart: 'Benefits of a dam' | 'Costs of a dam'

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a T-chart on the board: 'Benefits of a dam' on one side and 'Costs of a dam' on the other. Students are asked — before reading — to suggest anything they already know or believe goes in each column. The teacher accepts all ideas without judging and fills the chart with student contributions.

Students read the Dams section in the textbook and then write a response to the question on Textbook p. 27: 'What problems can arise after a dam is built? How can they be solved?' They work individually in their notebooks. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'The textbook mentions people and wildlife — have you thought about both?'

Whole-class discussion: the teacher revisits the T-chart on the board, inviting students to add new entries from the textbook section. The class is then asked: 'If you were the engineer deciding whether to build a dam on a river near your town, what question would you ask first?' Students discuss in pairs and share one question each. The teacher writes the questions on the board and asks the class to notice what values sit behind each question.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one explaining one benefit of dams and one explaining one cost, using the idea of trade-offs. The teacher closes by noting that India has more than 900 dams and that decisions about water storage are still being made today.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and explain the trade-offs involved in building a dam, recognising both benefits to water storage and costs to ecosystems and communities.
periods.section_context: Dam construction; reservoir; blocking river flow; storing water for dry seasons; drinking water from dams; irrigation from dams; electricity generation from dams; flooding of land by reservoirs; displacement of wildlife; displacement of people; more than 900 dams in India.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone heard of a place — a village or forest — that was submerged when a dam was built? What happened to the people or animals there?' This brings the displacement cost of dams into the room as a real human and ecological story.

periods.activity_title: Dissolving and Not Dissolving: The Pollution Experiment
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Students add sugar to one glass of water and cooking oil to another, stir both, observe which appears clear, and compare (p. 29)
materials: One spoonful of sugar per group
One spoonful of cooking oil per group

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a glass of clean water and asks: 'If I poured something into this water and you could no longer see it, does that mean the water is still clean and safe?' Students give quick yes/no answers and reasons. The teacher says the experiment will help them investigate this question.

Groups set up two glasses of water each. They add a spoonful of sugar to one and a spoonful of cooking oil to the other, stir both well, and observe as directed on Textbook p. 29. Students record in their notebooks: the appearance of each glass after stirring (clear or not), whether they can see the added substance, and what they conclude about which water looks clean. The teacher asks each group: 'Which glass would you feel safe drinking from — and why?'

Groups share their observations with the class. The teacher introduces the word solubility — 'sugar dissolved; oil did not' — and connects this to the section's point that some pollutants are invisible in water (dissolved) while others are visible (like oil), but both harm living things. The class discusses: what kinds of things from homes and factories might dissolve invisibly in river water?

Students write three lines in their notebooks: what they observed, what solubility means in their own words, and one example of a pollutant that might dissolve invisibly in a river. The teacher closes by connecting the experiment to the broader pollution theme in the chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple investigation to distinguish between substances that dissolve in water and those that do not, and connect this to the concept of invisible pollution.
periods.section_context: Sugar dissolved in water; cooking oil in water; solubility; invisible pollutants; visible pollutants (oil); river pollution from homes and factories.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'When you wash dishes or clothes with soap, where does that soapy water go in your home? Could it reach a nearby stream or river?' This connects the experiment directly to students' own household water use and waste.

periods.activity_title: What Litter Does to a River: Classifying Harm
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Students list things thrown in the waste bin at home or school and consider how each would harm animals, plants, and people if thrown into a river or pond (p. 29)
materials: Board or chart paper for class list
periods.visual_aids: Board table: 'Item | Who is harmed | How they are harmed'

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to think quietly for a short moment about what they threw away at home or school yesterday — wrappers, peels, paper, plastic bottles. Students call out items; the teacher lists them on the board without comment. The class ends up with a diverse list of everyday waste items.

Students open Textbook p. 29 for the task prompt. They pick five items from the board list and, in their notebooks, make a three-column table — Item | Who is harmed | How they are harmed — imagining each item thrown into a nearby river or pond. The teacher circulates and prompts specificity: 'When you write plastic wrapper, who exactly is harmed — a fish? A bird? A person drinking the water?' Students think through each case.

Pairs compare tables and together answer the textbook question from p. 28: 'Where do the plastic wrappers and bags that we litter end up?' They write a joint sentence. The class then shares the most interesting or surprising 'harm' they identified. The teacher builds a shared class table on the board, noting items that harm multiple groups.

Students reflect in two sentences: 'One item I will think twice about before throwing away is ___, because ___.' The teacher closes by connecting these everyday choices to the Namami Gange river-cleaning programme — organised efforts exist because individual actions accumulate.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and classify everyday waste by the type of harm each item causes to animals, plants, and people when it enters a water body.
periods.section_context: Plastic wrappers, bags, and litter entering rivers; waste and sewage from settlements; factories polluting rivers; harm to aquatic animals; harm to plants; harm to people drinking polluted water; Namami Gange programme.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen a stream, pond, or river near your home that has plastic or waste in it? What kinds of things are in it?' Affirm all observations — this grounds the classification task in real local water bodies students have seen.

periods.activity_title: Healthy River or Green Blanket? Comparing River Images
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Students compare two images of rivers — one healthy and one covered with algae — and explain the difference and its consequences (p. 30)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of healthy river versus algae-covered river (p. 30)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 30 and observe the two river images in silence. The teacher asks: 'Without reading any text, what do you notice is different between these two rivers? Write two observations in your notebook.' Students write quietly; the teacher does not give any information yet.

Students respond to the three questions from Textbook p. 30 in their notebooks: which river looks healthy and why; how so many plants can grow in water; and what happens when too many plants grow in a river. Students use the section text to support their answers. The teacher circulates and asks: 'What does the 'green blanket' do to the animals living under it?'

Whole-class discussion: the teacher uses the board to draw two simple water-body sketches — one with open water and one covered in algae — and students explain the difference using vocabulary from the section: fertiliser runoff, algal overgrowth, dissolved oxygen, aquatic life. The teacher asks: 'If the river near your town had this green blanket, what would you notice first?'

Students write a closing statement in their notebooks: 'The green blanket effect is caused by ___, and it harms rivers because ___.' The teacher affirms responses and notes that this is one type of pollution that is invisible in the sense that the fertiliser itself dissolves — connecting back to the previous experiment's idea of solubility.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare visual evidence of a healthy versus a polluted water body and explain the chain of cause and effect that produces algal overgrowth.
periods.section_context: Healthy river image; algae-covered river image; fertiliser runoff; algal overgrowth; green blanket effect; choking of aquatic life; water rendered undrinkable; dissolved oxygen loss.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you ever seen water that looked green or had a lot of plants floating on top near your home? What did it smell like? Did any animals or fish seem to live in it?' Lived observations of eutrophic water bodies ground this image-comparison activity in real experience.

periods.activity_title: Elders' Memory of Rivers: Then and Now
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Students discuss with parents or elders about the condition of water bodies near home when they were young and compare to the present (p. 28)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with the question from Textbook p. 28: 'Ask your parents or elders — what was the condition of water bodies near your home when they were your age, and what is the status today?' The teacher shares a brief example of change (a well that dried up, a river that narrowed) to model the kind of story being sought. Students are told to share what they know or have heard — there are no wrong answers.

Students share what they have heard from elders, older relatives, or community members about water bodies in their region — rivers, ponds, wells, stepwells — describing what they were like before and what they are like now. The teacher listens carefully, notes key contrasts on the board (deeper/shallower, cleaner/dirtier, full/empty), and asks follow-up questions: 'What changed? When did people notice the change starting?'

The teacher draws out the connection to the chapter's content: the changes students describe — more plastic, more foam, less fish, stronger smell — map onto specific causes the section names. Students identify which pollutant or cause might explain the change an elder described. This connects intergenerational testimony to scientific explanation.

Students write a reflection in their notebooks: 'The change in the water body near my home (or a place an elder told me about) is ___. One cause from what we have been reading that might explain this change is ___.' The teacher affirms the diversity of responses and closes by noting that memory and observation together are powerful ways of understanding environmental change.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect intergenerational testimony about environmental change to scientific explanations of river pollution.
periods.section_context: Condition of local water bodies in past versus present; elder testimony; pollution causes (waste, plastic, sewage, soaps and detergents); observable changes in water bodies over time.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone mention a well, a stepwell, or a baoli? What did elders say it was used for, and is it still used that way?' This surfaces traditional water structures and their changing status in an organic, unhurried way.

periods.activity_title: Three Actions to Protect Our Water
periods.section_ref: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
periods.textbook_anchor: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters — Students list three things they can do to protect the water bodies near them (p. 31)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a brief, direct question: 'Knowing everything we have discussed about what pollutes a river — what is ONE thing you personally can do, starting today, to protect a water body near you?' Students write one idea quickly in their notebooks. The teacher collects two or three responses and writes them on the board without comment.

Students open Textbook p. 31 and complete the task: list three specific actions they can take to protect water bodies near them. The teacher circulates and challenges vague responses: 'You wrote 'don't litter' — can you make that more specific? Where exactly, and what kind of litter are you thinking of?' Students revise their lists to be more concrete and personal.

In groups of four, students share their three actions and together choose the two that the group feels are most realistic and most impactful. Each group shares their chosen two with the class. The teacher builds a class list on the board and draws out a distinction: which actions are things one person can do alone, and which need community or school-level coordination?

Each student writes a personal commitment card in their notebook: 'I will [specific action] at [specific place] because [specific reason].' The teacher closes by connecting personal commitments to the chapter's broader message about river health depending on everyday choices made by many people.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and justify specific, realistic conservation actions to protect local water bodies.
periods.section_context: Three conservation actions for water bodies; individual versus community action; connection between everyday choices and river health; local water bodies.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a water body — a pond, river, or well — near your school or home that people in the community have taken care of together? What did they do, and who organised it?' This draws out community-level water stewardship stories as a complement to individual action.

periods.activity_title: Flood Consequences: Matching Problems to What They Affect
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Students match flood problems (dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, disease, damaged homes, schools shut) to what each affects (p. 32)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone ever seen a flooded road, a flooded field, or heard of a flood in your region? What did people say happened?' A few students share. The teacher notes that floods affect many parts of life at once and says the class will now map out exactly what gets disrupted.

Students open Textbook p. 32 and complete the match-the-columns activity individually in their notebooks: matching each flood problem — dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut — to what it affects — safe drinking, travel, food supply, lights and phones, people's health, shelter, and learning. The teacher circulates and asks students who have finished quickly to justify each match in a sentence.

The teacher checks the matches as a class, going through each pair. Where there is disagreement — for example, whether lost crops affects food supply or something else — the teacher facilitates a brief class debate rather than giving the answer directly. Students revise incorrect matches in their notebooks with a different colour or marking.

Students write a consolidating observation: 'A flood does not just damage one thing — it creates a chain of problems. The most serious chain I can see is ___.' The teacher closes by connecting the match activity to the section's point that deforestation worsens flooding because it removes the natural slowing of rainwater runoff.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the chain of consequences a flood produces across shelter, health, food, transport, and essential services.
periods.section_context: Flood problems: dirty water, broken roads, lost crops, no electricity, spread of diseases, damaged homes, schools shut; what floods affect: safe drinking, travel and transport, food supply, lights and fans and phones, people's health, shelter, learning; deforestation worsening floods.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In the match, 'lost crops' leads to 'food supply' — but who else is affected beyond the farmer? Who buys that crop? Who might go hungry?' This extends the matching into a chain-of-consequence discussion that deepens the systems thinking.

periods.activity_title: Flood Safety Role-Play: Leading the Response
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Floods — Students read the Flood Safety Tips and role-play as a Sarpanch or Municipal Corporator planning flood prevention, protection of elderly and disabled people, and safety of animals (p. 34)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 33 and read the Flood Safety Tips infographic covering before, during, and after a flood. The teacher gives them a short, unhurried reading period. After reading, the teacher introduces the role: 'You are the Sarpanch of a village or the Municipal Corporator of a city. A heavy flood warning has just arrived. What will you do first?'

Groups of four take on the role-play. Each group decides on one setting — village (Sarpanch) or city (Municipal Corporator). Using the Flood Safety Tips from Textbook p. 33–34 as their resource, they plan aloud what actions they will take to prevent flooding, prevent flood damage, keep elderly people and people with disability safe, and keep animals safe. One person in each group is the 'leader' making decisions, and the others are 'advisors' raising concerns. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'You have said move people — where will they go? Who will help them move?'

Two groups present their top three decisions to the class and explain why they made those choices. The class listens and then offers one addition or challenge. The teacher draws attention to how the same flood safety tips from the textbook were used differently for a village versus a city setting.

Each student writes one sentence in their notebooks: 'The most important action a community leader must take before a flood is ___, because ___.' The teacher closes by noting that civic preparedness — thinking ahead about what to do — is itself a form of safety.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present and justify a set of disaster-preparedness actions for a flood scenario, drawing on safety knowledge to protect vulnerable groups.
periods.section_context: Flood Safety Tips (before, during, after a flood); Sarpanch and Municipal Corporator roles; preventing flooding; preventing flood damage; keeping elderly people and people with disability safe; keeping animals safe; village versus city flood preparedness.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone's family or community ever prepared for or responded to a flood — or a very heavy rain that flooded roads or fields? What did people actually do?' Real community practices — moving cattle to higher ground, storing grain, blocking doorways — enrich the role-play with local knowledge.

periods.activity_title: When Water Runs Out: Imagining Drought
periods.textbook_anchor: When a River Runs Dry! — Students write what they would do if there was no water in their home for an entire day, then for a week (p. 35)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the question from Textbook p. 35 without any preamble: 'What would you do if you had no water in your home for an entire day?' Students write a quick personal response in their notebooks. The teacher then raises the stakes: 'Now imagine a whole week.' Students add to their response.

Students share their responses with a partner and then with the class. The teacher lists on the board the activities students say would be impossible or very difficult: bathing, cooking, drinking, flushing, cleaning. The teacher then asks: 'Where would you go to find water? Who might help you?' Students think about their own neighbourhood geography — a nearby shop, a tanker, a well, a relative's home.

The teacher introduces the examples from the section — Chennai's 2019 water crisis and the contrast with Bengaluru's 2022 floods — to show that both too much and too little water create emergencies. Students discuss: which crisis would be harder to manage in your own neighbourhood — a flood or a drought — and why? They write two reasons in their notebooks.

The teacher introduces the conservation habits from the section: turning off taps, fixing leaks, reusing water, the National Water Mission, and water ATMs. Students name one conservation habit they already follow or could start. The teacher closes by connecting personal water habits to the larger systems — rivers, reservoirs, and dams — that supply daily water.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the cascading effects of water scarcity on daily life and connect personal water use to the health of river systems.
periods.section_context: No water at home for a day; no water for a week; bathing, drinking, cooking, cleaning without water; Chennai 2019 water crisis; Bengaluru 2022 floods; migration when water runs out; conservation habits: turning off taps, fixing leaks, reusing water; National Water Mission; water ATMs.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you ever had a day when water did not come in the pipes, or when the water in your area tasted different or looked dirty? What did your family do?' This grounds the drought-imagination task in real lived water insecurity students may have experienced.

periods.activity_title: Designing a Water Filter: Simple Inquiry in Action
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students design a simple water filter using everyday materials and explain what they would include and why (p. 37)
materials: Plastic bottle or cup per group (cut in half)
Muddy or coloured water (prepared by the teacher by adding a little soil to water)

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows groups a cup of muddy water and asks: 'If this was the only water available to you — how would you make it cleaner using only things you can find at home or in school?' Students brainstorm in pairs and share ideas quickly. The teacher does not confirm or reject any idea yet — all suggestions are listed on the board.

Groups plan and build their simple water filter using the materials provided — cloth, sand, gravel, and a bottle or cup. Students refer to Textbook p. 37 for the prompt: what would they include and why? Each group writes a brief design rationale in their notebooks before building: what layer goes first, what each layer is meant to do. Groups then pour a small amount of muddy water through their filter and observe what comes out.

Groups compare outputs: whose filter produced clearer water? Why might different filter designs produce different results? The teacher draws out the reasoning: finer materials (sand, cloth) catch smaller particles; bigger materials (gravel) allow faster flow. Students connect this to the idea that clean water is the result of multiple filtration steps — in nature (soil, rock, sand) and in water treatment plants.

Students write a reflection in their notebooks: 'My filter worked best at removing ___, and it could not remove ___ because ___.' The teacher closes by asking: 'What does this experiment tell us about why keeping rivers free of dissolved chemicals — not just visible dirt — is so important?' This connects back to the solubility experiment from an earlier unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple filtration system, explaining the function of each layer and connecting physical filtration to the limits of removing dissolved pollutants.
periods.section_context: Simple water filter design; everyday materials (cloth, sand, gravel, plastic bottle); muddy water; filtration layers and their functions; limits of physical filtration for dissolved pollutants; clean water as a multi-step process.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen a clay pot, a sand filter, or a traditional method of purifying water used by older people in your family or village? What materials did they use?' This naturally surfaces traditional filtration knowledge as a point of comparison with the groups' own designs.

periods.activity_title: Journey of a River: Whole-Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students imagine planning a new city near a river and decide what steps to take to keep the river clean, prevent floods, and ensure water security (p. 37)
periods.visual_aids: Board mind-map: 'River' at centre with branches for source, life, livelihoods, dams, pollution, flooding, drought, conservation

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a circle on the board labelled 'River' and invites students to call out everything the chapter has taught them about rivers. As students call out ideas — source, tributaries, delta, perennial, livelihoods, dams, pollution, floods, drought, conservation — the teacher builds a whole-class mind-map branching out from the centre. The class sees the whole chapter's territory at once.

Students open Textbook p. 37 and work on the city-planning reflection: 'Imagine you are planning a new city near a river. What steps would you take to (a) keep the river clean, (b) prevent floods during heavy rains, and (c) ensure there is always enough water for everyone, even during summers?' Students write their plans individually, drawing on the full range of content from across the chapter — pollution causes, dam trade-offs, flood safety, conservation habits, water scarcity lessons. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'You have mentioned a dam — what trade-off would you also need to plan for?'

Four or five students read their city plans aloud. The class listens for: which ideas connect back to the natural strand (river source, forest, flooding, drought) and which connect to the human-cultural strand (livelihoods, sacred practices, dams, civic preparedness, conservation). The teacher names these two strands explicitly and asks: 'Can a good city plan ignore either strand?'

Each student writes one closing sentence: 'The most important thing I have learned about rivers is ___, and the one action I will take because of it is ___.' The teacher closes the chapter by returning to the opening image of the Godavari narrating its own journey — asking students: if the river could speak, what would it say about the choices people make?

periods.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of river systems, human dependencies, pollution, flooding, and conservation into a coherent plan that balances natural and human-cultural demands.
periods.section_context: Whole-chapter synthesis: Godavari river journey; source, tributaries, delta; perennial flow; river ecosystems; livelihoods (fishing, farming, ecotourism); dams and trade-offs; river pollution and conservation; floods and disaster preparedness; drought and water scarcity; local rivers; city planning for clean water, flood prevention, and water security.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If this chapter's river could write back to us after reading our city plans, what do you think it would say — is there anything important we forgot to plan for?' This closing question returns to the chapter's opening voice of the river and invites students to hold the river's perspective as a living system, not just a resource.

assessment_items.question_text: The Godavari river begins its journey at Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats. At which of the following does it end its journey?

options.label: A
options.text: The Arabian Sea

options.label: B
options.text: The Bay of Bengal

options.label: C
options.text: The Chilika Lake

options.label: D
options.text: The Indian Ocean

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This tests direct map-reading of the Godavari's terminal geography as studied from the textbook map.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Where I Begin, Where I Flow
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can extract and record geographical features of a river system from a labelled map.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused the Godavari's west-coast origin (Western Ghats) with the Arabian Sea, which receives rivers on the western side of the Ghats — a direction-of-flow confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has an imprecise mental map of where India's rivers meet the sea, not distinguishing between the specific named sea body (Bay of Bengal) and the broader ocean.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has associated a large water body name from Indian geography (Chilika Lake in Odisha) with the Godavari's terminal point — likely a confusion of eastward coastal geography.

assessment_items.question_text: The Godavari is called a perennial river. Which of the following best describes what 'perennial' means?

options.label: A
options.text: The river begins in a delta and ends at a mountain source.

options.label: B
options.text: The river flows only during the rainy season and dries up in summer.

options.label: C
options.text: The river flows throughout the year without drying up.

options.label: D
options.text: The river is the longest river in India.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. Tests the key conceptual distinction introduced in 'The Life I Hold'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between perennial and seasonal river systems and identify the ecosystems a perennial river sustains.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the definition — applying 'seasonal' features to a 'perennial' label. This is the central misconception the distinction is designed to address.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has conflated a length-based fact about the Ganga (longest river) with the word 'perennial', possibly because both are used to describe the Godavari's significance.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the geographical direction — a river's source is at a mountain and it ends at a delta or sea, not the other way around; this reveals a confused mental model of river geography.

assessment_items.question_text: People have built settlements near rivers since ancient times. Give two reasons why a river was essential for early settlements.
expected_elements: Identifies water for drinking and cooking as a reason.
Identifies at least one additional reason such as water for farming/irrigation, washing, or transport.
Uses the context of the river — not a general statement about water.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for two distinct, specific reasons grounded in river use. Partial credit for one correct reason stated clearly.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why human settlements historically developed near rivers by identifying the essential resources a river provides.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Identifies water for drinking and cooking as a reason.
Identifies at least one additional reason such as water for farming/irrigation, washing, or transport.
Uses the context of the river — not a general statement about water.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the table of occupations along the Godavari: fishing, farming, and ecotourism. Which occupation depends MOST DIRECTLY on the river being present and flowing?

options.label: A
options.text: All three occupations depend equally on the river.

options.label: B
options.text: Ecotourism, because visitors come to see the river scenery.

options.label: C
options.text: Farming, because soil near rivers is always rich.

options.label: D
options.text: Fishing, because the fish live in the river water itself.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. The item asks students to discriminate between direct and indirect river dependence. Ecotourism and farming are river-dependent but fish-harvesting requires the river as habitat. Accept reasoned justifications that correctly rank fishing as most direct.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the range of livelihoods and agricultural practices that depend directly on a river system.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identifies ecotourism as most direct — this reveals a surface-level association (ecotourists visit rivers) without analysing where the actual livelihood dependency lies.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has correctly identified farming as river-dependent but conflated 'rich soil' with the water source — a partial understanding that does not distinguish direct water dependency from soil fertility.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not attempted to rank or distinguish between the three occupations, suggesting undifferentiated thinking about river dependence.

assessment_items.task: Make a poster that shows at least four different ways people use a river. For each use, draw a picture and write a label explaining what the river provides.
assessment_items.scaffold: Divide your paper into four sections. In each section: draw one way people use the river; write a label for your drawing; write one sentence explaining what the river gives to people in that use.
format_of_output: A drawn and labelled poster on paper
At least four sections, each with a drawing and a written label
assessment_items.annotation: Assess for variety of river uses (not just drinking water), accuracy of labels, and clarity of the sentence explanation. A strong poster includes uses across categories: domestic (drinking, cooking), agricultural (irrigation), occupational (fishing), and other (ecotourism, industrial). Regional variation in river uses is expected and valid — accept any locally appropriate use of rivers as correct.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The Many Ways I Support Lives
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can communicate multiple ways a river system supports human life through a visual and labelled creative product.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether students can recall and visually represent the range of ways a river system supports human life, and communicate each use clearly through labelled drawing.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold divides the task into three manageable steps per section (draw, label, explain) so students are not overwhelmed. The teacher should confirm that students understand 'label' means a short naming word or phrase, and 'sentence' means a full statement of what the river provides.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four distinct uses drawn accurately (not four versions of 'drinking water'); labels are precise (e.g. 'rice farming' not just 'farming'); sentences explain the river's role (e.g. 'The river gives water for growing rice crops'). Weak: fewer than four sections, all uses clustered around drinking water, labels absent or illegible, sentences absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may use diagrams or symbols with labels. Students who find writing difficult may dictate their sentence to the teacher, who writes it under their drawing. Students whose regional rivers are used for different purposes (e.g. river sand for construction, river transport of goods) should be encouraged to include those local uses.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Poster with drawings and written labels
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The poster format directly mirrors the textbook activity and asks for a multi-modal output (visual + written) that makes the range of river uses visible at once — assessing both recall and communication.

assessment_items.question_text: A new dam is being planned on a river that flows through a forest village. The dam will store water for farming and generate electricity. Write a response in which you explain ONE benefit and ONE cost of building this dam, and suggest ONE way the cost could be reduced.
look_for: Names a specific, accurate benefit of the dam (e.g. water storage for dry season irrigation, electricity generation, drinking water supply).
Names a specific, accurate cost (e.g. displacement of village residents, flooding of forest and wildlife habitat, loss of agricultural land upstream).
Offers a realistic suggestion for reducing the cost (e.g. relocating displaced families with compensation, protecting a wildlife corridor, creating alternative habitat).
Uses reasoning rather than assertion — the response explains why the benefit matters and why the cost is a problem.
Does not dismiss either the benefit or the cost — both are treated as real.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for responses that identify a specific benefit, a specific cost, and a realistic mitigation, all reasoned rather than listed. Partial credit for any two of the three elements. Accept regional or local examples of dams that students may know about — these are valid and stronger evidence of understanding.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Dams—Storing My Water, Changing My Flow
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and explain the trade-offs involved in building a dam, recognising both benefits to water storage and costs to ecosystems and communities.

Names a specific, accurate cost (e.g. displacement of village residents, flooding of forest and wildlife habitat, loss of agricultural land upstream).
Offers a realistic suggestion for reducing the cost (e.g. relocating displaced families with compensation, protecting a wildlife corridor, creating alternative habitat).
Uses reasoning rather than assertion — the response explains why the benefit matters and why the cost is a problem.

assessment_items.question_text: In an experiment, sugar was stirred into one glass of water and cooking oil was stirred into another. After stirring, one glass appeared clear and the other had a visible layer. Which glass appeared clear, and what does this tell us about whether that water is safe to drink?
expected_elements: Correctly identifies the sugar-water glass as appearing clear.
Explains that 'clear' does not mean safe — the sugar (or a dissolved substance) cannot be seen but is present in the water.
Connects this to the idea of invisible pollutants that dissolve in river water but still cause harm.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for correctly identifying the sugar-water glass as clear AND explaining that clear appearance does not mean the water is safe. Partial credit for correct identification without the safety inference.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the sugar-water glass as appearing clear.
Explains that 'clear' does not mean safe — the sugar (or a dissolved substance) cannot be seen but is present in the water.
Connects this to the idea of invisible pollutants that dissolve in river water but still cause harm.

assessment_items.question_text: A plastic wrapper is thrown into a river. Which group of living things is most directly harmed when the plastic breaks into tiny pieces in the water?

options.label: A
options.text: Birds flying over the river

options.label: B
options.text: Farmers irrigating fields far from the river

options.label: C
options.text: Fish and other aquatic animals living in the river

options.label: D
options.text: Trees growing on the river bank

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. Tests whether students can apply their classification of harm to a specific scenario. Fish and aquatic animals are most directly harmed when plastic enters the water column.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and classify everyday waste by the type of harm each item causes to animals, plants, and people when it enters a water body.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has extended harm to flying birds — a plausible chain effect (birds eating fish that ate plastic) but not the most direct harm. This reveals chain-thinking without precision about 'most directly'.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has connected plastic pollution to farming, which is an indirect and distant harm — suggesting confusion about which parts of the ecosystem are inside versus outside the river water column.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has identified bank-side trees as the harmed group — a confusion between bank-side vegetation and aquatic life, possibly because both are 'near' the river.

assessment_items.question_text: A river that was once clear and full of fish now has a thick green layer covering its surface. Explain what caused this green layer and what it does to the river's aquatic life.
expected_elements: Identifies fertiliser runoff from farms as a cause of the green layer.
Explains that excess fertiliser causes algae to grow rapidly, covering the water surface.
Explains that the algal layer blocks sunlight or uses up dissolved oxygen, harming or killing fish and other aquatic life.
Uses the term 'algal overgrowth' or 'green blanket effect' or equivalent.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for responses that correctly identify fertiliser runoff as cause, describe algal overgrowth, and explain the harm to aquatic life. Partial credit for identifying the cause without explaining the harm mechanism.

expected_elements: Identifies fertiliser runoff from farms as a cause of the green layer.
Explains that excess fertiliser causes algae to grow rapidly, covering the water surface.
Explains that the algal layer blocks sunlight or uses up dissolved oxygen, harming or killing fish and other aquatic life.
Uses the term 'algal overgrowth' or 'green blanket effect' or equivalent.

assessment_items.question_text: An elder in your family tells you that the pond near your home used to be very clean and full of fish when they were young, but today it smells bad and the fish are gone. Using what you have read about river and water body pollution, explain two possible reasons for the change and what could be done to help the pond recover.
look_for: Identifies two distinct, specific causes of water body deterioration (e.g. plastic and waste dumped near the pond; untreated sewage from growing settlements; detergent or chemical runoff; fertiliser causing algal growth).
Links each cause to an observable effect described by the elder (bad smell, fish disappearing).
Suggests at least one realistic recovery action (stopping waste dumping, treating sewage, community clean-up, no chemical washing near the pond).
Connects the elder's testimony to scientific explanations from the chapter rather than treating them as unrelated.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any locally plausible causes the student identifies — regional variation in pollution sources is expected and valid. A strong response integrates the elder's observation with chapter content; a weak response lists causes without connecting them to the testimony or chapter knowledge. Regional variation note: the specific causes will vary by the student's locality (coastal pond, river pond, urban pond) and all region-specific causes are acceptable.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect intergenerational testimony about environmental change to scientific explanations of river pollution.

assessment_items.task: Think of a river, pond, or water body near your home or school. Write three specific actions YOU will take to help keep it clean. For each action, explain exactly where you will do it and why it will help.
assessment_items.scaffold: Action 1: I will ___ at/near ___ because ___. Action 2: I will ___ at/near ___ because ___. Action 3: I will ___ at/near ___ because ___.
format_of_output: Three written action statements following the scaffold
Each statement names a specific action, a specific place, and a reason
assessment_items.annotation: Assess for specificity (vague actions like 'keep rivers clean' are not sufficient), realistic location (the place named must be somewhere the student could actually act), and reasoning (the 'because' must link the action to a pollution cause or conservation principle from the chapter). Regional variation note: the specific water body and actions named will vary by the student's locality — any locally appropriate water body and conservation action is valid.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Pollutes Me and Why it Matters
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and justify specific, realistic conservation actions to protect local water bodies.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether students can translate chapter knowledge about water pollution and conservation into specific, justified personal actions grounded in their own local context.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold's three-part structure (action + place + reason) ensures students go beyond vague intentions. The teacher should prompt students who write 'I will not litter' to add where exactly and what specific litter they mean.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three distinct actions (not three versions of 'not littering'), each anchored to a specific real place (named stream, school tap, market drain), each with a reason linked to a chapter concept (e.g. 'because plastic breaks into pieces that fish eat'). Weak: generic actions without place or reason; all three actions are the same type.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who do not live near a visible water body may write about actions at home (fixing a dripping tap, not pouring chemicals down the drain) — these count as valid conservation actions that protect water sources indirectly. Students who struggle with writing may draw their three actions with labels.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The written-commitment format mirrors the personal commitment activity in the unit and requires students to commit in concrete language rather than abstract principle — making conservation observable and assessable.

assessment_items.question_text: During a flood, roads are broken and people cannot travel. Which part of daily life is MOST DIRECTLY affected by broken roads?

options.label: A
options.text: Food supply, because crops are lost in the flooded fields.

options.label: B
options.text: Learning, because schools are shut due to flooding.

options.label: C
options.text: People's health, because dirty water spreads diseases.

options.label: D
options.text: Travel and transport, because people and goods cannot move.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. Tests direct recall and application of the match-the-columns activity. Broken roads map directly to travel and transport.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the chain of consequences a flood produces across shelter, health, food, transport, and essential services.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has associated a flood consequence (health, dirty water) with broken roads — correctly identifying a flood effect but not the direct match for broken roads specifically.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has associated broken roads with food supply, possibly because both are flood consequences — but this conflates broken roads with flooded fields, which are different flood problems.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has associated broken roads with school closure — a plausible chain effect (children cannot travel to school on broken roads) but not the primary direct effect named in the match-the-columns activity.

assessment_items.task: You are the Sarpanch of a village that has received a flood warning. Write a short announcement telling villagers THREE actions they must take to stay safe — one action BEFORE the flood arrives, one action DURING the flood, and one action AFTER the flood has passed. For each action, say why it is important.
assessment_items.scaffold: BEFORE the flood: [action] — This is important because ___. DURING the flood: [action] — This is important because ___. AFTER the flood: [action] — This is important because ___.
format_of_output: A written announcement in three parts (before, during, after)
Each part names an action and a reason
assessment_items.annotation: Assess for accuracy of the action relative to the flood phase (an action listed under 'before' must genuinely be a preparedness action, not a response action), specificity of the action, and quality of the reason. Strong responses draw on the Flood Safety Tips from the textbook. Accept regionally appropriate variations in flood safety actions — in coastal, river-plain, and hill-region contexts, the specific safety actions will differ.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present and justify a set of disaster-preparedness actions for a flood scenario, drawing on safety knowledge to protect vulnerable groups.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether students can apply flood safety knowledge from the Flood Safety Tips to a civic leadership scenario, organising actions correctly by flood phase and justifying each.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-phase scaffold (before, during, after) mirrors the Flood Safety Tips infographic structure from the textbook. The teacher should confirm that students understand the difference between preparedness (before), response (during), and recovery (after) actions.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three actions correctly placed in their phase (e.g. 'store clean water' before, 'move to higher ground' during, 'boil water before drinking' after); each reason explains the harm avoided by the action. Weak: actions placed in wrong phases (e.g. 'build a dam' as a during-flood action), no reasons given, or all three actions are the same type.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing lengthy announcements difficult may use bullet-point format. Students who find the Sarpanch framing unfamiliar may write from their own perspective ('I would tell my family to...'). Both formats are acceptable as long as the three-phase structure and reasons are present.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The announcement format requires students to communicate safety information to others — testing both knowledge and the ability to communicate it in a civic context, which mirrors the role-play activity of the unit.

assessment_items.question_text: In 2019, the city of Chennai faced a severe water crisis because its rivers and reservoirs had run dry. Explain two ways in which daily life in Chennai would have changed during this crisis, and describe two conservation habits that could help prevent such a crisis in another city.
look_for: Identifies two specific and distinct impacts on daily life when water runs out (e.g. cannot cook or drink without sourcing water elsewhere; cannot bathe or clean; schools or businesses disrupted; families forced to travel far to collect water or buy from tankers).
Links each impact to a specific daily activity that depends on water.
Names two specific conservation habits (e.g. turning off taps while brushing, fixing dripping taps, reusing washing water for plants, storing rainwater).
Explains why each conservation habit reduces water use or protects water supply.
Responses show awareness that water scarcity is a systemic problem requiring both individual and collective action.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for two specific impacts reasoned in relation to daily activities, and two conservation habits with explanations. Partial credit for any three of the four elements. The Chennai example is used as a prompt — students need not know details of the 2019 crisis beyond what the chapter provides.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the cascading effects of water scarcity on daily life and connect personal water use to the health of river systems.

assessment_items.question_text: A group of students built a water filter using layers of gravel, sand, and cloth. After pouring muddy water through, the water came out clearer but still had a faint colour. Explain why the filter made the water clearer, and give ONE reason why it is still not fully clean.
expected_elements: Explains that the gravel, sand, and cloth layers trap or block solid particles (mud, dirt) — making the water appear clearer.
Explains that the filter cannot remove dissolved substances (chemicals, dyes, invisible pollutants) — these pass through the filter layers.
Uses the concept of physical filtration versus dissolved pollutants to justify why the water is clearer but not fully clean.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for correctly explaining both the mechanism of filtration (trapping solids) and its limit (cannot remove dissolved substances). Partial credit for explaining filtration without the limit, or naming the limit without the mechanism.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple filtration system, explaining the function of each layer and connecting physical filtration to the limits of removing dissolved pollutants.

assessment_items.question_text: You are planning a new city near a river. The city will need clean drinking water, safe housing, and protection from both floods and drought. Using what you know about how rivers work, how people depend on them, and the problems they face, write a plan that addresses all three needs. Explain how your plan keeps the river healthy at the same time.
look_for: Addresses clean drinking water — names a realistic supply strategy (e.g. water treatment, conservation habits, dam or reservoir with consideration of trade-offs).
Addresses flood protection — names a realistic structural or behavioural measure (e.g. avoiding building too close to the river bank, planting trees to slow runoff, flood early warning systems).
Addresses drought resilience — names a conservation or storage measure (e.g. rainwater harvesting, water ATMs, reducing wastage, the National Water Mission principle).
Explains at least one step that protects river health (e.g. no untreated sewage into the river, no plastic waste near the river, keeping forests along river banks).
The plan is internally coherent — the steps do not contradict each other.
The response draws on content from across the chapter rather than from a single section alone.
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item draws on content from all major sections of the chapter. Full credit for responses that address all three needs with at least one specific and reasoned action each, and that include a river-health step. Partial credit for addressing two of the three needs well. Accept regionally influenced plans — students in flood-prone areas may weight flood protection more heavily, and students in drought-prone areas may emphasise conservation more. Both emphases are valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can integrate knowledge of river systems, human dependencies, pollution, flooding, and conservation into a coherent plan that balances natural and human-cultural demands.
